workflow: 1. Start with lightweight exploration (5-10 steps): use grep, find, and cat to locate relevant files and understand the issue scope. 2. Form a concrete hypothesis about the root cause and required changes by step 10-12. 3. Make your first edit by step 15 at the latest—use sed -i for line changes or cat <<EOF for file creation; do not continue exploring past step 15 without editing. 4. After any edit, immediately verify it was applied correctly (cat the changed lines, use git diff), then run the repository's test command within 3-5 steps (pytest, python -m pytest, ./manage.py test, npm test, etc.). 5. Read the test output and iterate: if tests fail, make a targeted follow-up edit and re-test; if tests pass, verify edge cases or submit. 6. Submit only after confirming tests pass: run echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT as a standalone command. 7. If blocked with 'EXPLORATION BUDGET EXHAUSTED', immediately attempt an edit using your best hypothesis—test failures provide more signal than further reading. 8. If blocked with 'EDIT VALIDATION REQUIRED', run tests immediately before any further exploration.
context_strategy: Keep the conversation history focused on the current edit-test cycle. After each test run, summarize what the test revealed (which assertions failed, what error messages appeared) in your next thought section to maintain continuity. Do not rehash earlier exploration findings once you have made an edit—focus thoughts on interpreting test results and planning the next fix iteration. If you need to re-examine a file after a test failure, state explicitly why that file is relevant to the failure. Avoid repeating the same grep or find commands; if you already located a file, reference that knowledge and move to editing or testing. When the harness injects a blocking message, treat it as a hard constraint and immediately shift your action to satisfy it (edit if exploration budget exhausted, test if validation required).
submission_strategy: Before submitting, verify: (1) You have made at least one file edit addressing the reported issue. (2) You have run the repository's test suite or relevant test file and observed the output. (3) The test output shows the specific failing test case from the issue now passes, or the error described in the issue no longer occurs. (4) You have checked for obvious regressions by running broader tests if time permits. (5) You have used git diff or cat to confirm your edits are actually present in the files. Do NOT submit if you have only explored and read files without editing. Do NOT submit immediately after an edit without running tests. Do NOT submit if the last test run showed failures related to your changes. If uncertain whether tests passed, run them one more time before submitting. The submission command (echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT) must be issued alone, not combined with other commands.
hints: The harness enforces two hard blocking rules: (1) After step 15 without any edit, all exploration commands (grep, find, cat, ls, sed -n) are blocked until you perform a file-editing command (sed -i, cat <<EOF, redirection with >, python scripts that write files). (2) After any edit, you can explore for up to 5 steps, then all further exploration is blocked until you run a test command (pytest, python -m pytest, python -m unittest, ./manage.py test, npm test, cargo test, go test, etc.). Recognize these blocks and respond immediately—they will repeat on every turn until you comply. Common test commands by repo type: Django uses ./manage.py test or python tests/runtests.py; pytest-based repos use pytest <file> or python -m pytest; Node repos use npm test. If the test command is not obvious, check for a tests/ directory, look for a runtests.py or test runner script, or examine CI config files (.github/workflows, tox.ini). When editing with sed -i, always view the target lines first (sed -n '10,20p' file.py) because line numbers shift after edits. For multi-line changes, prefer cat <<'EOF' > file to rewrite entire small files or functions. Remember that directory changes (cd) do not persist; prefix commands with cd /path && your_command if needed. The harness will reject responses with multiple bash code blocks—issue exactly one command per turn.
budget_guidance: Allocate your step budget as follows: steps 1-10 for initial exploration (locate files, understand structure, read the issue-relevant code); steps 11-15 for forming a hypothesis and making the first edit; steps 16-25 for the first edit-test cycle (verify edit, run tests, read output); steps 26-40 for iteration (refine edits based on test feedback, re-test, handle edge cases); steps 41-50 for final validation and submission. Do NOT spend more than 10-12 steps on initial exploration—if you are still only reading files at step 15, you have over-explored and the harness will block you. After each edit, budget at most 3-5 steps for quick verification reads before running tests; do not re-explore the entire codebase. If you hit the step-15 block, do not panic—make your best-guess edit immediately using the information you have; test failures will guide the next iteration more effectively than additional reading. If you hit the post-edit test block, run tests immediately even if you are uncertain about the test command; trying a test command and seeing an error is better than being blocked. Reserve the final 5-10 steps for confirming tests pass and submitting; do not submit in a rush without test confirmation. If you are iterating well (edit at step 12, test at step 16, second edit at step 20, test at step 23), you are on track. If you reach step 30 without having run tests, you are off track—force a test run immediately.
